# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been uncomfortable, but climate change has transformed it from a seasonal nuisance into a genuine public health crisis. Heat now kills more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the toll falls disproportionately on city dwellers. This is not an accident of geography but a product of design. Cities concentrate heat: asphalt absorbs solar radiation all day and releases it at night, buildings block cooling breezes, air conditioners pump hot exhaust into streets, and the dearth of vegetation eliminates the natural cooling that shade and evaporation provide. The good news is that these design choices can be revised. Cities that treat heat as a design problem—rather than an act of God—can dramatically improve summer livability, though every intervention involves tradeoffs that residents must weigh together.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: planting trees. A mature street tree does several things at once. Its canopy blocks solar radiation before it ever reaches the pavement, making the space beneath it feel ten to fifteen degrees cooler.
